rv.q: Stephen Brown-Fried adapts and directs the rarely produced Shakespeare works outstandingly, with a stunning 16-member NAATCO cast.
This lesser-performed of the Bard’s works gets a stunning reimagination by NAATCO (American Theatre Company) in Henry VI: A Trilogy in Two Parts.
If “Henry VI” hasn’t proven as big a draw through the years, this juicy adaptation certainly presents a good argument for revisiting it more often.

The blinding revelation of Stephen Brown-Fried 's production is that Henry VI , a round robin of intrigues, tribalism, backstabbings, loveless political marriages, frivolous wars, populist rebellions, and acts of torture, is the uncanny mirror of the present day.
In any case, I think the show deserves my tapping back into my initial youthful enthusiasm.
While following the plot and the characters is a challenge, the story with its scandals and betrayals proves to be very modern and may remind you of modern politics.
The production can do nothing with the plays’ shortcomings, though.
This production attempts to make that connection, but only succeeds half-way.
Five hours fly by in this gripping, emotionally rich adaptation.
But you have to get through Part I of this Shakespeare marathon first, and not only is it longer, it’s duller.
The fight choreography, by Orlando Pabotoy and Kimiye Corwin is athletic and genuinely thrilling.

cn.t: Critics praise this ambitious revival of Shakespeare's rarely staged trilogy, commending the strong ensemble performances and Stephen Brown-Fried's gripping adaptation that makes the epic political saga emotionally engaging across its substantial runtime.

vr.q: this production couldn't quite turn the play into a prince, but its shortcomings were mostly in the play itself
